card.title: Potential and Kinetic Energy of the Satellite

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Gravitational potential V = −GM/r is the work per unit mass to bring a test mass from infinity; potential energy U = −GMm/r is the negative binding energy of two masses. Near the surface U ≈ mgh. The field relates to the potential by g = −dV/dr, and circular orbits have total energy E = −GMm/2r, confirming their bound nature.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Gravitational potential: V = −GM/r (J/kg)
Gravitational potential energy: U = mV = −GMm/r (J)
Near the surface: U = mgh (h ≪ R)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ 'Potential and potential energy are the same.' ✅ Potential V is work per unit mass (J/kg); potential energy U = mV (J). V belongs to a point in the field; U belongs to the mass–field system.  ·  ❌ 'Negative energy is unphysical.' ✅ Negative potential energy simply means the system is BOUND — energy must be added to separate it. It is a matter of the reference at infinity.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Both V and U are defined with reference zero at infinity — that is why they are negative.  ·  Use U = mgh only for small heights (h ≪ R); use −GMm/r for space-scale problems.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: V at Earth's surface: V = −GM/R = −6.25×10⁷ J/kg.  ·  U of 1000 kg satellite at r = 6.8×10⁶ m: U = −GMm/r = −5.9×10¹⁰ J.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ 'U = mgh and U = −GMm/r disagree.' ✅ They agree for small heights: mgh is the CHANGE in −GMm/r near the surface. Use the right one for the régime.  ·  ❌ 'Potential is maximum at Earth's surface.' ✅ Potential is most negative at the surface (−GM/R) and rises toward zero with altitude — at infinity it reaches the (higher) value 0.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Derive V and U starting from F = GMm/r² by integration.  ·  Solve 5 numericals for V and U at various distances.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Escape-energy shortcut: energy to infinity = GMm/R = mgR (since g = GM/R²).  ·  Orbital energy memory: E = −GMm/2r = U/2 means K = −U/2.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Calculate the gravitational potential at a point 3×10⁷ m from the centre of Earth (M = 6×10²⁴ kg).  ·  Find the gravitational potential energy of a 1500 kg satellite at an altitude of 2000 km above Earth.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Derivation of U = −GMm/r from integrating F = GMm/r² is a standard question.  ·  Numericals on satellite total energy and escape energy are frequently asked.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Gravitational potential V = −GM/r is scalar work per unit mass.  ·  Gravitational potential energy U = −GMm/r equals the negative binding energy.  ·  Near the surface U = mgh; far away use −GMm/r.  ·  g = −dV/dr links the vector field to the scalar potential.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: V = −GM/r is negative, approaching zero at infinity.  ·  U = −GMm/r is the energy of the (bound) system, negative for attraction.  ·  Near Earth's surface U = mgh is the appropriate approximation.  ·  Potential and field connect: g = −dV/dr.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Gravitational potential energy is exactly the 'missing' energy that binds systems — this is why the binding energy of Earth + satellite equals |U|.  ·  The concept of potential is useful because it is scalar: complex many-body problems reduce to addition rather than vector resolution.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: How much energy is required to move a 3000 kg spacecraft from Earth's surface to infinity?  ·  A 700 kg probe is moved from r = 8×10⁶ m to r = 5×10⁶ m. Find the change in its potential energy.  ·  Derive that for a circular orbit v² = GM/r and hence E = −GMm/2r.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Conceptual MCQ: why is potential energy negative? → because zero is at infinity and gravity is attractive.  ·  Linking g = −dV/dr to a V–r graph slope appears in higher-level questions.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Escape energy per kg: GM/R = 6.25×10⁷ J ≈ 17 kWh per kg.  ·  Near surface: a 2 kg mass lifted 10 m gains U = mgh = 196 J.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: The gravitational potential at a point at distance r from mass M is: → B  ·  Gravitational potential energy of two masses m and M at distance r is: → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Gravitational potential V:** the work done per unit mass in bringing a test mass from infinity to a point, without acceleration. For a point mass M: V = −GM/r. At infinity V = 0, and everywhere else V is negative because gravity does positive work as the mass approaches — the field does the work, so potential decreases.  ·  **Gravitational potential energy U:** the work done against gravity in assembling a system; for two masses separated by r: U = −GMm/r. It is the energy of the whole system, not of one mass alone. U is negative because the system is bound — you must supply GMm/r of energy to separate the masses to infinity.  ·  **Why the minus sign matters:** potential energy is defined with zero at infinity. Since the force is attractive, energy is released (and PE decreases) as masses come together. A satellite in orbit at radius r has U = −GMm/r — its total mechanical energy is E = K + U = −GMm/2r, which is negative, confirming a bound orbit.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Circular orbits are bound: E_total = −GMm/2r = U/2.  ·  Field from potential: g = −dV/dr  ·  Total orbital energy: E = −GMm/2r = U/2

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Total energy of a circular orbit is negative: E = −GMm/2r.  ·  ❌ 'Doubling the distance doubles the potential energy.' ✅ U = −GMm/r — doubling r halves the magnitude, so U becomes −GMm/2r (less negative).  ·  ❌ 'A satellite far away has lots of potential energy.' ✅ A far-away satellite has potential energy near ZERO (least negative, but U ≈ 0). It needs enormous kinetic energy (orbital speed) that comes from the launch energy.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Total energy of circular orbit: E = −GMm/2r — negative, so the orbit is bound.  ·  Potential is a scalar — use scalar addition with multiple masses.  ·  The escape energy equals |U| at the surface: GMm/R.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: NEB may ask 'derive U = −GMm/r starting from F = GMm/r²' — know the integration step.  ·  V = −GM/r (potential) and U = −GMm/r (potential energy) both take zero at infinity — hence negative for attracted masses.  ·  Near Earth's surface use U = mgh; for space-scale distances use the inverse-r form.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: The field is the negative slope of the potential: g = −dV/dr.  ·  Binding energy of a two-mass system = |U| = GMm/r.  ·  Total energy of a circular orbit (E = −GMm/2r) is negative — a signature of a bound state.
